name: Ningdong (traditional Chinese herbal formula)
short: Small trials in children with ADHD or Tourette's (8 weeks to 6 months): loss of appetite, constipation; fewer side effects than methylphenidate; no liver or kidney changes. Ingredients not reported.
text: The safety evidence comes from small, short randomised trials in children, and none of the abstracts lists the formula's ingredients. In an 8-week double-blind trial in 72 children with ADHD, Ningdong granule caused fewer side effects than methylphenidate, and the authors reported it safe and tolerable as monitored by blood, urine and stool tests and liver and kidney function; the authors noted that a systematic study of its safety was still lacking. In an 8-week placebo-controlled trial in children and adolescents aged 7 to 18 with Tourette's disorder, two children taking the granule reported loss of appetite and one constipation, with no significant changes in laboratory tests or physical examinations. A randomised trial in 120 patients with Tourette syndrome reported no liver or kidney damage in children given the granule. In two Tourette syndrome trials the granule was also given together with haloperidol: one found the combination more effective and safe than the other groups, and in a 6-month trial in 90 children adverse reactions occurred in 13.3% given the granule plus haloperidol compared with 36.7% given haloperidol alone; the abstracts do not describe what those reactions were. No interaction data were found in the cited sources, and the abstracts do not report safety beyond 6 months.
